fixes.explanation: Jerusalem it is. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles (Ezekiel 1:1–3), up between earth and heaven and carries him there in visions of God (Ezekiel 8:3). No walking, no packing, no asking if we're there yet. I got carried once myself, from a kitchen counter to the back of a junk drawer, and that trip took a hand and a slammed drawer.

Samaria is a real place, friend, but it's not where the Spirit takes Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles (Ezekiel 1:1–3). The text says he's carried in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the north gate of the inner court (Ezekiel 8:3). Everything he sees from here on happens in that city. Keep Jerusalem in your apron pocket.

Bethel is a real place too, but the Spirit doesn't carry Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles (Ezekiel 1:1–3), there. The text says he's taken in visions of God to Jerusalem, to the entrance of the north gate of the inner court (Ezekiel 8:3). That's where the whole scene happens. Bethel stays out of this one.

That's the one. The text says the idol that provokes jealousy was seated at the entrance of the north gate of the inner court (Ezekiel 8:3). God then tells Ezekiel to lift his eyes to the north, and he sees this idol of jealousy in the entrance north of the Altar Gate (Ezekiel 8:5). So Ezekiel sees it twice.

No golden calf shows up in these verses, friend. The text says the idol that provokes jealousy was seated at that gate (Ezekiel 8:3). God even points Ezekiel to it again, north of the Altar Gate (Ezekiel 8:5). The text calls it the idol that provokes jealousy, so that's the name to hold onto.

The bronze serpent isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. What sits at the entrance of the north gate of the inner court is the idol that provokes jealousy (Ezekiel 8:3). God draws Ezekiel's eyes to it again, north of the Altar Gate (Ezekiel 8:5).

The tablets of the law aren't in this scene, friend. The text says Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel, like the vision he had seen in the plain (Ezekiel 8:4). My mustache reached for the tablets too, so you're in good company. But the text puts the glory right there in Jerusalem.
That's right. God says, “Yet you will see even greater abominations.” (Ezekiel 8:6). The idol at the gate isn't the end of the tour, friend. Ezekiel has only just started walking.

That's not what God tells him. Right after pointing out the idol, God says, “Yet you will see even greater abominations.” (Ezekiel 8:6). Nothing in these verses says the people turn back, friend. What's coming next is more abominations.

The text says the opposite, friend. God doesn't tell Ezekiel to peek. He tells him, “dig through the wall.” and Ezekiel does (Ezekiel 8:8). Digging a hole through a wall is real work, and my mustache would need a nap after.

The prophets of Baal aren't in this room. The text says seventy elders of the house of Israel stand before the engravings (Ezekiel 8:11). Jaazaniah son of Shaphan is named as standing among them. These are Israel's own elders, and I think that's what stings.

The text says the opposite. God tells Ezekiel what they're saying: “The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). They say He does not see. They say it in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol.

That's right, it's false. The elders are saying, “The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). They say it while they're in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol. I think the darkness is part of the picture.
Forsaken is the word. The elders say, “the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). That's what they say, in the darkness, each at his own idol's shrine. Those are their words, friend.
Cleansed isn't the word they use. The elders say, “the LORD has forsaken the land.” (Ezekiel 8:12). That's the line God repeats to Ezekiel in that dark room. The right word here is forsaken, friend.

Not priests this time. The text says Ezekiel sees women sitting at the north gate of the house of the LORD, weeping for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). Tammuz is a false god. After a room full of elders, I'll admit priests feel like the next guess, friend, but the text says women.

No soldiers are named at this gate, friend. The text says Ezekiel sees women sitting at the entrance of the north gate of the house of the LORD, weeping for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). Tammuz is a false god.

False is right. About twenty-five men stand between the portico and the altar, but they have their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east (Ezekiel 8:16). So they're turned away from it. I think that's the detail to notice.

The sun, yes. About twenty-five men have their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east, and they're bowing in worship of the sun (Ezekiel 8:16). It's a sad sight, friend. I'll just say it plainly.

That's it. God asks if the abominations they practice there aren't enough, “…that they must also fill the land with violence and continually provoke Me to anger?” (Ezekiel 8:17). So it's the whole land, not just the temple. Violence in the land is what God names, friend.

That's what the text says. God says, “Therefore I will respond with wrath. I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them.” (Ezekiel 8:18). I won't joke about this one, friend. Take a quiet breath before the next one.

That's not what God says here. He says, “Therefore I will respond with wrath. I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them.” (Ezekiel 8:18). Nothing in the verse offers more time. The verse says wrath and no pity, friend.
True. God says, “Although they shout loudly in My ears, I will not listen to them.” (Ezekiel 8:18). That's the last line of the passage. Let it sit a moment, friend.
